newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian debt futures rocket, looking for easing.
newsitem.headline: Australian debt futures rocket, looking for easing.

text.p: FUTURES CASH YIELD
*Australian debt futures screamed ahead after an extremely weak set of labour force data reinforced speculation that a further cut in official interest rates is on the cards.
*May employment slumps 40,300, unemployment up to 8.8 pct.
Australian debt futures roared ahead after an extremely weak set of labour force data reinforced speculation that a further cut in official interest rates is on the cards.

September bills struck 92.88, indicating a cash rate of 5.12 percent compared with 5.5 percent official rates, while three-year bond futures jumped to their highest level since February 1994 at 94.16.
Employment slumped 40,300 in May. Median forecasts had centred on a 15,000 rise. Unemployment rose to 8.8 percent against a generally expected 8.7 percent.
("And) if it hadn't been for the participation rate coming down the unemployment rate would be over 9.0 percent," said Stephen Roberts, chief economist at UBS Australia.
The participation rate was 63.2 percent and down from 63.5 percent in April.

"We hear (the authorities) talking about the need for growth, but they are not going to get it with figures like this. Look what they have got on the table now," said Annette Beacher, senior economist at Citibank Australia. "...It's time to get off the fence and start thinking that they (the RBA) will cut again."
At best the economy remains patchy with the housing sector showing strength as seen in Wednesday's 12.2 percent jump in housing finance for April.
But retail trade in April recorded its first double negative since July/August 1993 and today's employment data was the largest monthly fall since April 1993.
And even taking into account the last official interest rate cut on May 23, Westpac's consumer and National Australia Bank's business sentiment surveys painted a picture of gloom.
"From now on, it puts us on 9.30 (a.m.) watch," said UBS's Roberts, referring to the time the RBA makes any rate changes.

"This (employment) data is very, very soft, but there are risks in all this as well. Yes they can bring rates down again, but they will have to put up with the rollercoaster that comes after it, because some of the stronger sectors will go from not just strong to boom," Roberts added, pointing the housing market.

While the debt market's strength was pointed at the short end, it also dragged 10-year bond futures higher taking equivalent bond yields to closer to 7.0 percent, which was briefly breached in early December last year.

The yield curve steepened sharply on the data and yield spreads to the the U.S. and Canada tumbled. The Australian/U.S. 10-year spread breached resistance at 65 basis points to narrow to its lowest level in over three years.
